timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

2	
3	Read: CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md (a retrospective of an earlier app; nothing in it bears on this issue),
4	docs/remote-client.md §4.1, §4.3, §4.4, §5, §9, the "Remote client" status section of docs/design.md
5	(starts at line 3107), and the code below. Line numbers are from this worktree (branch
6	`dispatch/230-...`, HEAD 7fe8949). I ran nothing and opened no browser.
7	
8	## On-disk record and rehydration (before the pane)
9	
10	Nothing new has to be stored for the first cut. The page is data compiled into the binary; the state is already durable:
11	
12	- `identity.json` (`Identity`: server_id, name, certificate DER base64, `spki_sha256`, listen). The key is in the
13	  Keychain under `remote-key:<server_id>` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95` `make_identity`, `src/app.rs:2783` `load_identity`).
14	- `devices.json` (`PairedDevice`, `src/ports/remote.rs:96`): id, name, scope, **token SHA-256 only**, created, last_seen.
15	  A browser is a row of the same shape. Its token is stored by the host only as a hash, so the browser's copy is its only
16	  copy; this is the rehydration question. Today the token reaches the client in the `/pair` body (`src/app.rs:3606`
17	  `remote_pair`, reply keys `token, scope, server_id, device_id`). The device keeps it. For the page, "rehydrate" means:
18	  reload the page, present the same credential (cookie, or whatever storage Decision 2 picks), read `/api/v1/*` again.
19	  The pairing window itself is never saved (`core/remote.rs`, `pairing_at`); a restart closes it.
20	- Revocation = delete the row (`AppAction::RevokeDevice`), and the next request 401s (`authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3127`)
21	  and the device's socket closes (test `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket`, tests/remote.rs:2892). The page's "revoked"
22	  state is therefore a 401 `unauthorized` "the token is not known; pair again" from any `/api/v1` call. The host cannot tell
23	  "revoked" from "never paired" or "key rotated" on a 401 (same body); "identity changed" is only detectable client-side,
24	  by `/info.spki_sha256` or `server_id` differing from what the page remembered (or `server_id` equal and key different).
25	  A rotated key deletes every device (docs §5, `identity_rotated`), so the page's stored credential just 401s.
26	- Nothing in the page's state is read by the core. Per CLAUDE.md the core stays deterministic, so serving static files
27	  is an adapter/app concern, not a core one.
28	
29	## Where the issue touches the code
30	
31	Serving the page
32	- `src/app.rs:3017` `serve_remote`: line 3023 `strip_prefix("/api/v1/")` else `refuse(404 not_found)`. This is the one place
33	  a non-API path is refused; `GET /` and static files must be answered before it. The match at 3028 is the API allowlist.
34	- `src/adapters/remote.rs:360` `RemoteRequest` and `RemoteReply` (389): `RemoteReply` is `{status, body, authenticated}`
35	  only. **There are no response headers and no content type.** `respond` (530) hard-codes `Content-Type: application/json`,
36	  `Connection: keep-alive`, and a fixed reason table (no 302/304/etc.). Static files, `Set-Cookie`, CSP, `Cache-Control`
37	  and `Content-Type: text/html` all need a header channel on `RemoteReply` (additive; 30 construction sites of
38	  `RemoteReply {` across src and tests, so a `Default`/constructor helps) or a path decided in the connection thread
39	  before the frame is asked.
40	- `read_request` (444) keeps only: method, path, query (undecoded), body, bearer, upgrade key. It **drops every other
41	  header**: no `Cookie`, no `User-Agent`, no `Origin`, no `Host`, no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, no `Accept-Encoding`. Each
42	  one the plan wants must be added to `RemoteRequest` (CLAUDE.md: the bearer is taken out of the headers so it is never
43	  logged with them, so a cookie must get the same treatment). `MAX_HEAD` is 8 KiB (437).
44	- Query values are "undecoded: ids and numbers only" (line 377 doc). The URL form carries `code` (Crockford, safe), `key`
45	  (hex), `id` (uuid), all URL-safe, so decoding is not needed for these, but the doc comment's promise would be amended.
46	- `connection` (770): per-connection loop; `Limits::limited` (631) only rate-limits the exact paths `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and
47	  `/api/v1/info` (60/min). Any other path, including a new `/` or `/app.js`, is **not rate limited at all** today.
48	  The unauthenticated pool is 4 connections (`MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED`, 567), counted per TCP connection until the first
49	  reply with `authenticated: true` (810 on). A browser opens several parallel connections to load `/`, `.css`, `.js`, `/info`
50	  (typically up to 6 per host) with keep-alive; that can fill the 4-slot unauthenticated pool and the accept loop silently
51	  drops the rest (`bind`, 690-700). Which pool a page load counts against follows from this code: all of it is
52	  "unauthenticated" until a request answers `authenticated: true`; static-file replies are `false` unless the plan changes that.
53	  Idle timeout 30 s (573) holds a slot from a browser that keeps a connection open.
54	- The `ANSWER_TIMEOUT`/frame hop: every request, including a static one, goes over the 64-deep channel to the frame, drained
55	  8 per pass (`serve_pending`, src/app.rs:1572). Serving a page this way costs frame passes; answering static paths on the
56	  connection thread would not, but then they bypass the frame's refuse/log path. Plan's call; both are in the tree.
57	- `local_address()` (adapters/remote.rs:962) picks one outbound IPv4/IPv6 source address; it is not bracketed for a URL.

59	Pairing and the QR

61	  variable), makes the QR from the same string (`qr_texture`, 254 on), and "Copy invite" copies the same text. Address is

63	  (`listen.lan` false, `bind_remote` at src/app.rs:2938) the QR still shows the LAN address, which nothing answers; a phone
64	  scan would fail. The dialog's checkbox text says "only paired devices get past /info" (ui/remote.rs ≈ line 108) and will be

66	- `core/remote.rs`: pairing window state, `OpenPairing{code, scope}`, `PairingFailed` (three wrong closes it), `new_device`.
67	  The code is 8 chars, 40 bits (`pairing_code`, adapters/remote.rs:325), single use; `Paired` consumes it. The device name

69	  (not retained, see above), so "Safari on iPhone" must come from the page (`navigator.userAgent`/`userAgentData`) or from a
70	  new `RemoteRequest` header field. The page choosing its own name is the same trust as any device.
71	- `remote_pair` (3606) requires `spki_sha256` in the body to equal the host's. A browser page cannot compute the key of the
72	  certificate it is talking to (no JS API); it can only compare the URL's `key` with `/info.spki_sha256`, which the **host
73	  itself** returns, so that comparison proves only that the URL's key matches whatever answered. This is what the issue

76	  = `Wire.decode(JSON)`; `client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:107-125` takes either `<invite json>` (one argument) or

78	  (`ReconcileTests`, `EventTests`, `DraftTests`, `NewSessionTests`, `FixturesTests.swift:161` with a fixture `client/Fixtures/pin.json`/`pair.json`).
79	  A URL accepted there means a `parse` that tries URL first, then JSON; the `addresses` array becomes one entry from the URL authority.

1	# Facts for #230, a web control surface
2	
3	No spike was run. The one question a spike could answer (a real browser against a real certificate) needs a device or a browser session, so it goes to the owner. Evidence covers sources read 2026-10-22. Tree line numbers are from HEAD 7fe8949.
4	
5	## Settled
6	
7	### The tree
8	
9	- The `/pair` reply and every other reply are wrapped by `envelope`/`envelope_at` as `{epoch, revision, body}`. Errors carry `{epoch, revision, error:{code,message}}`. (src/app.rs:3717-3751)
10	- `send` takes a JSON body `{op, text}`. `op` is 1 to 64 characters and `text` is 1 byte to 16 KiB, both trimmed. Anything else is 400 `bad_request`. A device without `control` scope gets 403 `scope`. A body that is not JSON gets 400. A failed send starting `interrupted` gets 409 `interrupted`. `resume` and `trust` take only `op`. (src/app.rs:3159-3216)
11	- Nothing checks `Content-Type` on a POST body. The body is parsed with `serde_json::from_slice` (src/app.rs:3175). A cookie-authenticated `send` therefore has no CSRF defence in the tree today. No `Origin` check exists either (investigation notes).
12	- The headset's paste path is `BrowserView.swift:849` ("Paste the QR code's text") to `PairingInvite.parse` at line 883. `boot(invite:)` at line 105 also calls `parse`. `parse` is `Wire.decode` of JSON (client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:114-116). The consumers of the JSON form are `PairingInvite.parse`, `switchboard-remote pair` (main.swift:107-125, one argument or `<host:port> <code> <spki>`), `ConnectionManager.pair(invite:)` and the Swift tests. Decision 3 can be built on that: one `parse` that accepts a URL first, then JSON, covers all of them. The three-argument CLI form needs no change.
13	- The Rust UI test asserts the invite is JSON with `code`, `spki_sha256` and an `addresses` array (tests/ui.rs:7485-7492). It does not assert the "only paired devices get past /info" hover text (src/ui/remote.rs:113). Changing the payload to a URL changes this test. The hover text is only a string to amend.
14	- `Cargo.toml` has only `exclude = ["vendor/egui_term"]` (line 91). There is no `include` list, so a root-level `web/` is not dropped. `include_str!` embeds the files at compile time, so the bundle is unaffected.
15	- `SessionView` has no excerpt field. The card's excerpt is computed in `src/ui/cards.rs` `agent_excerpt`, from conversations and pane captions that live in `UiState` (investigation notes, grep of `control/src/lib.rs` found none). "Each with the one-line excerpt" is therefore a new read model. The alternatives are `last-response` per session, or showing `card` and `waiting_reason` only. The plan chooses; the gap is a fact.
16	- `RemoteRequest` keeps no `Cookie`, `User-Agent`, `Origin` or `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. `RemoteReply` has no header channel and `respond` hard-codes `application/json`. `respond_upgrade` writes no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. Only the exact paths `/api/v1/pair` and `/api/v1/info` are rate-limited. The unauthenticated pool is 4 connections. All of this is from the investigation notes (adapters/remote.rs:360-570, 631, 843).
17	
18	### The web
19	
20	- **HSTS does not apply to an IP-literal host.** A user agent must not note an IP literal as a known HSTS host and must not match one on load. Click-through is blocked only for known HSTS hosts. A page addressed by `https://<ipv4>:<port>/` therefore keeps the ordinary click-through interstitial, and "HTTPS-First" upgrades do not remove it. RFC 6797 §8.1.1, §8.3, §8.4, §12.1: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6797#section-8.1
21	  - Queries: `Chrome "Proceed to" unsafe self-signed certificate IP address HSTS no proceed link "thisisunsafe"`.
22	  - Covers: the RFC as published. The `thisisunsafe` posts are forum leads and are not evidence.
23	- **An IP host is matched against `iPAddress` entries in subjectAltName.** `commonName` is a deprecated fallback. Chrome has ignored the CN since version 58 and the certificate is rejected as `ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID`. Apple's server-certificate rules say the same for DNS names: the SAN is required and the CN is not trusted. The host's certificate has no SAN at all (`CertificateParams::new(vec![])`, adapters/remote.rs:95), so every browser will report a name mismatch beyond "self-signed". Whether the interstitial still offers a proceed link for that combination is not settled (see Unresolved).
24	  - Sources: https://cabforum.org/working-groups/server/guidance-ip-addresses-certificates, https://support.apple.com/en-us/103769, the Chromium-58 reports in the first search below.
25	  - Queries: `Chrome Firefox Safari self-signed certificate IP address no subjectAltName ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID proceed anyway`; `RFC 6125 OR "Baseline Requirements" IP address certificate must be in subjectAltName iPAddress not commonName browsers`.
26	  - **Consequence:** a certificate that lists the address(es) it is served on, as `iPAddress` entries, is a precondition for any browser path, whichever way Decision 1 goes. Address changes (DHCP) would then mean reissuing, which `identity.json` and the key rotation rule (§5) must account for.
27	- **A click-through exception does not reliably cover `wss://`.**
28	  - Firefox: Mozilla bug 1187666 (Firefox 39, WONTFIX) says "we don't create dialogs for failed subresources, which is what wss is". The stored exception is the only route, and the workaround is to visit the host and port over `https://` first. https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1187666
29	  - Safari: WebKit bug 41419 is NEW and unassigned. Safari fails `wss://` to an untrusted certificate with no console message, and works once the certificate is trusted. https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419
30	  - iOS 26 beta 3: a developer on Apple's forums reports `wss://192.168.1.81/…` failing with "The certificate for this server is invalid" after the page's warning was accepted. The poster later wrote "seems to be resolved in Beta 5". No Apple statement. https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/792842
31	  - Because the page and the socket are the same origin (same host and port), the Firefox workaround is satisfied by the page load itself. The remaining risk is Safari and iOS, where only the user-trusted-certificate path is known to work.
32	  - Queries: `iOS Safari self-signed certificate "visit this website" WebSocket wss fails after accepting certificate warning`; `Firefox "Add Exception" self-signed certificate wss WebSocket must accept certificate for websocket port separately`.
33	  - **Consequence:** the plan must give the page a polling fallback (`GET /api/v1/*` with the revision counter) that works when the socket cannot connect, and must say so on the page. This is the line the plan builds to under Decision 1, whichever way it goes.
34	- **Browsers cannot set a header on `new WebSocket()`.** The constructor takes a URL and an optional list of subprotocols. Browsers send `Origin`, and `Cookie` for the origin. https://websocket.org/reference/headers/, https://blog.openreplay.com/websocket-authentication/ (leads that agree with RFC 6455 §4.1 item 8). Query: `browser WebSocket constructor cannot set Authorization header Sec-WebSocket-Protocol token cookie Origin check`.
35	- **Sec-WebSocket-Protocol, from RFC 6455 §4.1 and §4.2.2** (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#section-4.1):
36	  - Values are `1#token`, characters U+0021 to U+007E excluding separators, and unique. A 43-character base64url token is a legal value.
37	  - If the client offered subprotocols and the server's reply omits the header, the connection is not established (§1.9).
38	  - A reply that selects a protocol not offered fails the connection.
39	  - A subprotocol route therefore needs `respond_upgrade` to echo one offered value, and the token sits in a request header that the tree must keep out of logs.
40	- **Origin on the upgrade:** browser clients must send `Origin`. Browsers do not apply CORS to WebSockets, so the server decides. If the server does not validate `Origin`, it accepts connections from anywhere. A missing `Origin` should not be read as a browser (RFC 6455 §4.1 item 8, §4.2.1 item 7, §4.2.2). A cookie credential on the socket therefore requires an `Origin` check against the host's own origin, and the same applies to `POST` (CSRF). A header-carried token (subprotocol) does not need one.
41	- **Cookies are not isolated by port.** "If a cookie is readable by a service running on one port, the cookie is also readable by a service running on another port of the same server." A cookie named for this host is sent to any other service on the same IP regardless of port. `Secure` protects only confidentiality in transit, and `HttpOnly` limits the cookie to HTTP requests. RFC 6265 §8.5, §4.1.2.5, §4.1.2.6: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6265#section-8.5. The `SameSite=Strict` effect on other ports is not separately sourced here; the port-blindness above is the relevant half. A `__Host-` prefix needs `Path=/`, `Secure` and no `Domain`; it does not add port isolation (not sourced here, a lead from general knowledge). Query: none beyond the RFC fetch.
42	  - **Consequence:** a token cookie on an IP host is readable by every other service the owner runs on that IP, for example the dev servers Dispatch starts. The subprotocol or storage routes do not have this reach.
43	- **`history.replaceState` replaces the current history entry's URL in place** (same-origin only). Back navigation then shows the replaced URL. MDN says nothing about `Referer`, so `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on the page stays a separate, cheap measure. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/replaceState. Not sourced: the camera app's own link preview or an in-app webview keeping the original URL in its own history.
44	- **Certificate validity limits:** Apple's 825-day limit is stated for TLS server certificates that chain to a root and issued after 2019-07-01. The page does not say whether it applies to a user-trusted self-signed certificate; it covers neither the year-4096 `notAfter` nor a self-signed leaf. That is not settled; see Unresolved. https://support.apple.com/en-us/103769. Query: the same page fetch only.
45	
46	## Unresolved
47	
48	1. **Does each browser offer a proceed link for a self-signed, no-SAN, IP-literal certificate?** Tried: the two searches under the SAN claim and the Firefox and WebKit bug pages. The sources cover the name error but not the proceed link, and one WebKit comment (bug 158345) was a search snippet only. Plan: assume the click-through exists on Chrome and Firefox (HSTS does not apply to IP hosts) and still add the IP to the SAN. If favourable, the plan may state click-through as the trust step. If not, the plan must offer the certificate download (a new public path serving data already in the handshake) and say so. Both branches need the SAN work, so the plan builds it unconditionally.
49	2. **How long iOS or macOS Safari remembers an exception, and whether Safari/iOS applies it to `wss://` today.** Tried: `Safari iOS "This Connection Is Not Private" "visit this website" self-signed certificate asks again…`. No source states a duration. WebKit 41419 is open and the iOS 26 report is one forum post that later cleared. Plan: write the polling fallback and the "reconnecting / trust the certificate" state regardless. If it works, the socket is the primary path; if not, polling is.
50	3. **Whether the iPhone or Android camera opens `https://<ip>:<port>/?code=…&key=…&id=…`, and in which browser.** Tried: `iPhone camera QR code opens https URL with IP address and port local network Safari self-signed`. Only generic or low-quality pages returned, and a 2018 bug about `@` in URLs, which this URL does not contain. Plan: the page works when the URL is typed or pasted as well, and the pairing window keeps "Copy invite" with the URL. If the camera opens it, the issue's acceptance test is as written. If it does not, the copy path is the way in.
51	4. **Does a year-4096 `notAfter` or a missing SAN hit an OS limit if the owner installs the certificate as a trusted profile?** Tried: Apple's certificate-requirements page, silent about user-installed leaves. Plan: if the certificate download is picked, issue the certificate with a SAN and a validity within 825 days, and renew it. That also costs nothing if click-through works.
52	5. **Does an unauthenticated page load stay inside the 4-connection pool?** This is a tree-runnable behaviour but the question is "does a browser's parallel loading fit", and no browser is available in this session. By the code, every connection is unauthenticated until a reply sets `authenticated: true`, a browser opens up to six per host, the accept loop drops over-pool connections silently, and idle connections hold a slot for 30 s (adapters/remote.rs:567-573, 690-700, 810). Plan: bundle the page into as few files as practical, send `Connection: close` on static replies (or answer them on the connection thread without a slot), and test pool use with the host's own client. This holds whichever way a browser behaves.
53	
54	## For the owner
55	
56	1. **Do the owner's phone, iPad and other Mac browsers show a proceed option for the host's certificate once it has a SAN, and does the page's socket connect after it?** Needs their devices and the signed bundle's identity.
57	   - If yes, the click-through is the trust step. Say it in the paired-devices dialog and keep polling as the fallback.
58	   - If no, the plan must serve the certificate for download and say how to trust it on each device. The plan adds the SAN work and the polling fallback in both cases.
59	2. **Which address does the owner reach the host by (IP, `<name>.local`, IPv6 link-local, a guest network that isolates clients)?** `local_address()` picks one interface (adapters/remote.rs:962) and returns it unbracketed.
60	   - If the answer is one stable IPv4, the plan puts that IP in the SAN.
61	   - If it varies, the plan must allow several SAN entries and bracket IPv6 in the URL. In both cases the QR still shows the LAN address when the port is bound to loopback only; the plan must hide the QR then.

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). Envelope:

```json
{
  "server_id": "uuid",
  "epoch": "uuid",
  "revision": 1042,
  "type": "changed",
  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
  "at_ms": 1760220000000
}
```

Event types:

- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker r
- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collectio
- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.

**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:

1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved
2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose rea
   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key withi
3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what 

**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's r

**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app b

**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:

1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
4. enables commands.

## Remote client (2026-10-12)

A native visionOS and iPadOS client that browses the sessions and
working sets of several running Switchboard installations and sends
prompts to them is specified in `docs/remote-client.md`: a port over
the control port's wire contract, pairing with a pinned host key, one
revision counter and `changed` events, and content work off the frame
thread. The plan is Spike 22 and then Milestone A as five commits.

Built so far:

- **A0, the conversation cache in the app.** Parsed transcripts moved
  from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp::conversations`
  (`content::ConversationCache`): each entry keeps the handle and file
  time it was read through, `is_current` answers the refresh without a
  read, and the views reach the cache through `DrawCtx::conversations`.
  A seeded conversation (tests, the script) has no handle and no file
  time and is never read over. Behaviour is unchanged; the UI tests
  seed the new place.

# Plan: a web control surface on the remote port (#230)

The host serves a small browser page from the remote port. A phone, an
iPad or another Mac pairs from a URL that carries the code and then lists
the sessions, shows one, and sends a reply. One commit. The README and the
remote status section of `docs/design.md` are updated in it. The app runs
at every step.

"The facts" below is `facts.md` for this ticket. "Settled", "Unresolved"
and "For the owner" are its headings. Line numbers are from this worktree
at HEAD 7fe8949.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **"each with ... the one-line excerpt the card shows."** The wire has no
  excerpt. `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637`) carries `card`,
  `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `liveness`, `quiet_secs`, `last_activity_ms`
  and `prompt_refusal`, and nothing else a card says. The excerpt is
  computed in the UI from `UiState` caches (`agent_excerpt`,
  `src/ui/cards.rs:558`, and the pane captions), which the core never
  holds (facts, Settled, "The tree"). The issue also says "no new read
  model unless the page cannot do without one", and the page can: a row
  shows kind, the card's word, the waiting reason and how long it has been
  quiet. The excerpt is a follow-up (end of plan), because it needs a core
  field that the UI and the port would share.
- **"the browser then trusts that certificate for that address."** The
  tree does not bear it out. The certificate has no `subjectAltName`
  (`CertificateParams::new(vec![])`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:95-100`), and
  a browser matches an IP host against SAN entries only (facts, Settled,
  "An IP host is matched against `iPAddress` entries"). Chrome-family
  browsers report a name error on top of "self-signed". Whether a proceed
  link is then offered is Unresolved 1. A click-through exception also does
  not reliably cover `wss://` on Safari and iOS (facts, Settled, "A
  click-through exception does not reliably cover `wss://`"). The plan
  therefore puts the address in the certificate, gives the page a polling
  path, and serves the certificate for download. Click-through is the
  stated trust step, not an assumption the build rests on.
- **Spec lines the plan amends.** `docs/remote-client.md` §5 says the token
  is "sent only as a bearer header ... never in a URL", that pairing is
  required "before anything but `/info` and `/pair`", and that "every
  later request ... the host answers with the device's scope". The first
  two change because the issue asks for them (cookie transport, the page
  served before pairing). The third is not true of the tree: `envelope`
  (`src/app.rs:3730`) carries `epoch`, `revision` and `body` only, so the
  page has no way to learn its scope. That is the one new read the plan
  adds, `GET /api/v1/device`.
- **The issue's `https://<address>:<port>/` with `local_address()`.** The
  address comes from a connected IPv4 UDP socket (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962`),
  so it is never IPv6 and never needs brackets today. The URL builder
  brackets an IPv6 literal anyway, since the owner may reach the host
  another way (For the owner 2).

## The record

`workspace.json` and `views.json` are untouched, so `SCHEMA_VERSION`
(`src/core/model.rs:12`, 16 today) and `VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION`
(`src/core/model.rs:612`, 7 today) do not move.
`devices.json` is untouched. A browser is a `PairedDevice` like any other:
a name, a scope, the token's hash. The browser's copy of the token is an
`HttpOnly` cookie (below), so the host's store of hashes is still the only
other copy and rehydration is "reload the page, the cookie rides the first
request".

`identity.json` gets one field.

- `Identity.addresses: Vec<String>` (`src/ports/remote.rs:27`,
  `#[serde(default)]`), the IP addresses and names the current certificate
  lists in its `subjectAltName`. It is how the host knows, without parsing
  its own DER, whether the certificate still covers the address a phone
  would use.
- `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` (`src/ports/remote.rs:16`, 1 today) becomes
  the value there at implementation time, plus one, since a ticket landing
  in parallel may take the next number first. `identity.json` has no
  `migrate` step and no reader checks the version, so `serde(default)` is
  the whole migration: an old file reads with `addresses` empty, which the
  next bind treats as "not covered" and reissues once.

**The certificate is reissued over the same key, never a new one.** The pin
is the SPKI hash and `Identity.spki_sha256` already says so (a certificate
"reissued over the same key still verifies", `src/ports/remote.rs`), and
the native `Pin` verifier ignores names and validity
(`src/adapters/remote.rs:183-200`). So adding a SAN changes no pairing and
clears no `devices.json`. This is not key rotation (§5), and
`identity_rotated` stays false.

- `remote::make_identity` builds the certificate with SAN entries
  `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1` and the current `local_address()` when
  there is one, and records them in `addresses`.
- New `remote::reissue_certificate(identity, key_pem, addresses)` signs a
  new certificate with `rcgen::KeyPair::from_pem`, asserts the SPKI hash
  is unchanged, and returns the identity with the new `certificate` and
  `addresses`. `not_after` stays as it is (year 4096, comment at
  `src/adapters/remote.rs:90`): shortening it is a spec decision, not this
  ticket's (follow-up 3).
- Address changes: `SwitchboardApp::refresh_certificate` compares
  `local_address()` plus the loopback names with `identity.addresses`. It
  runs at the start of `bind_remote` (`src/app.rs:2936`), and on `Tick`
  while the pairing window is open, which is the only time a phone needs
  the current address. A mismatch reissues over the key from the secret
  store (`identity.key_account()`), dispatches
  `AppAction::CertificateReissued(identity)`, and, outside `bind_remote`,
  calls `bind_remote` again so the listener serves the new certificate. A
  read-only instance does neither. Any live socket on the port drops on
  that rebind. A device must reconnect, which is the cost of a DHCP change
  and is the same as toggling the LAN checkbox today.

## The signals

No new event. The page reads the signals the headset reads, per
`docs/remote-client.md` §4.4: `hello {epoch, revision}`, `changed`,
`removed`, `resync_required`, the `watching` answer, and the close of the
socket on revocation. It applies replies by revision: subscribe first,
fetch snapshots, refetch a resource whose event revision is past its
snapshot's, and a refetch of everything after `resync_required` or a new
`epoch`.

New refusals the page and the native clients can see:

- `403 origin`: a request authenticated by the cookie whose `Origin` is
  missing (for a non-`GET` or an upgrade) or is not the host's own origin.
- `401 unauthorized` is unchanged and is the page's only "revoked" signal.
  The host cannot tell revoked from never-paired from rotated on a 401
  (`authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3127`), so the page decides the wording
  client-side. It remembers `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}`, not a
  credential, in `localStorage` (guarded by `try/catch`; it must render
  without it). A 401 with `/info` showing the same `server_id` and key says
  "this device was removed on the host, pair again". A different key or id
  says "identity changed, pair again" and sends nothing. A 401 with nothing
  remembered says "not paired".
- A socket that does not open within 4 s, or closes with no 401 behind it,
  moves the page to polling (see the UI) and says so on the page. This is
  the fallback the facts require whichever way Safari and iOS behave
  (Unresolved 2).

## The actions and effects

### Serving the page

The page is three files under a new root-level `web/` directory,
`index.html`, `app.css` and `app.js`. They are embedded with
`include_str!` in a new `src/adapters/web.rs`. `Cargo.toml` has only an
`exclude` for `vendor/egui_term` (line 91), so `web/` needs no list entry
and the bundle is unaffected (facts, Settled).

**Static paths are answered on the connection thread, before the frame.**
`docs/remote-client.md` §4.1 says the frame does core state only, and a
file is not core state. In `connection` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:770`),
after the rate check and before `requests.try_send`, a `GET` of `/`,
`/app.css` or `/app.js` is answered by `web::asset(path, host)`. Any
other method on those paths is `405`. Every other path outside `/api/v1/`
still reaches `serve_remote` and gets its existing `404 not_found`
(`src/app.rs:3023`). The exact set of paths outside `/api/v1/` is those
three and nothing else. A query on `/` is ignored by the host and never
logged (`read_request` splits it off, and `refuse` logs method and path).

Each asset answer carries:

- `Content-Type`: `text/html; charset=utf-8`, `text/css; charset=utf-8`,
  `text/javascript; charset=utf-8`.
- `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self';
  style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'self' wss://<host>;
  base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`. There is
  no inline script and no inline style, and no external resource, so the
  HTML has no `style=`, no `on*=` and no `<script>` body. `<host>` is the
  request's `Host` header filtered to `[A-Za-z0-9.:\[\]-]`, because older
  WebKit does not match `wss:` against `'self'`. I have not verified that;
  the explicit entry is cheap and does no harm if it is unneeded.
- `Cache-Control: no-store`, so a new build never meets an old script.
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`.
  The latter keeps a `?code=` URL out of any `Referer`; `replaceState`
  (below) deals with the history and says nothing of `Referer`.
- `Connection: close`, and the connection thread ends after the write.

**Pool and rate window.** A page load counts against the unauthenticated
pool of 4 (`MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:567`), because
every connection is unauthenticated until a reply says otherwise
(`reply.authenticated`, line 810) and a static reply says `false`. That
pool is not enlarged: it is §4.1's bound. `Connection: close` returns the
slot at once, where a keep-alive would hold it for `IDLE_TIMEOUT` (30 s,
line 573) and let one browser starve a second device. The page is three
requests before its first `/info`, with at most two of them concurrent,
and the script keeps at most two API requests in flight until the first
authenticated reply arrives (Unresolved 5; the behaviour of a real
browser's parallel connections is for the implementer's manual run).
`Limits::limited` (line 631) gets a third window, `assets`, 120 a minute
for every path outside `/api/v1/`, so the unauthenticated static paths and
junk are bounded as `/pair` (6) and `/info` (60) are.

### Credentials: a cookie, not storage or a subprotocol

Decision 2. **The `/pair` reply sets an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict;
Path=/; Max-Age=34560000` cookie named `sb_session`, and the page's
script never holds the token.** This is the safer of the stores. A token in
`localStorage` or `sessionStorage` is readable by any script on the origin,
and one cookie-less XSS in a page that renders terminal text would hand it
over. An `HttpOnly` cookie cannot be read by script at all. A
`Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value would have the script holding the token on
every load.

What the cookie costs, stated plainly: cookies are not isolated by port
(RFC 6265 §8.5; facts, Settled), so `sb_session` is sent to every other
service the owner runs on the same IP, and one of them could replay it
against this port. The cookie is bounded by the scope the owner picked
(the dialog defaults to read-only) and dies when the device is revoked. It
is the price of the choice and the dialog says so (UI). It is not
mitigated further here.

**The mechanics are Unresolved, so they are the first thing built and
tried.** The tree and the facts do not say whether browsers store and send
a `Secure` cookie, over `fetch` and over `wss://`, for an origin they
accepted by click-through (facts, Unresolved 2 covers the socket, nothing
covers the cookie). The implementer's first step (Build order, step 3) is
a real-browser check of exactly that: pair, reload, and the cookie rides
`fetch` and the socket. If it fails, the fallback is a follow-up ticket,
not a second transport in this commit. The page would show its "cannot
keep a login in this browser" state and nothing else would ship half-built.

Host changes (`src/adapters/remote.rs`, `src/app.rs`):

- `RemoteRequest` (line 360) gains `host: Option<String>`,
  `origin: Option<String>` and `session: Option<String>`. `session` is the
  value of the `sb_session` cookie only. `read_request` (line 444) drops
  every other cookie, because a cookie reaches this port from every other
  service on the IP and none of them is ours. As the bearer is, the cookie
  is taken out of the headers so it is never logged with them. There are 3
  `RemoteRequest {` literals (`grep` count) to update.
- `RemoteReply` (line 389) gains `headers: Vec<(String, String)>`, and
  `respond` (line 530) writes them, a `Content-Type` among them replacing
  the default. A constructor `RemoteReply::plain(status, body,
  authenticated)` stands for the current literal. There are 30
  `RemoteReply {` sites in `src` and `tests`, all converted mechanically
  to it.
- `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127`) takes the bearer when there is one and
  otherwise `request.session`, with a bearer winning over a cookie. When
  the credential is the cookie, the request must pass the origin test:
  any `Origin` present equals `https://<Host>`, and a non-`GET` or an
  upgrade also requires one. A failure is `403 origin`, logged by method
  and path only. This closes cross-site `POST .../send` and cross-site
  WebSocket hijacking, for which the tree has no defence today (nothing
  checks `Origin` or the POST `Content-Type`, `src/app.rs:3175`; facts,
  Settled). A bearer request needs none: a header cannot be forged
  cross-site. `Origin` is compared with a port, so another service on the
  same IP with the cookie cannot pass it.
- `remote_pair` (`src/app.rs:3606`) takes an optional body field
  `session: "cookie"`. With it, the reply omits `token` and carries
  `Set-Cookie`, and the request must pass the same origin test (a cookie
  is only ever set for a same-origin page). Without it, nothing changes
  for the native clients: the reply is `{token, scope, server_id,
  device_id}` as now. The device name is the body's `device_name`, which
  `new_device` trims to 64 characters (`src/core/remote.rs:169`). The host
  cannot see a user agent (not retained), so the page sends the name it
  makes from `navigator.userAgent`, for example "Safari on iPhone".
- New `GET /api/v1/device` (`serve_remote`, after `authenticate`) answers
  `{device_id, name, scope}`. It is additive on the allowlist, and
  `capabilities` in `remote_info` (`src/app.rs:3580`) gains `"device"`.

### The certificate for download

Decision 1. **Click-through is the trust step the dialog states, and the
host also offers its certificate**, because the two are not alternatives
the build can choose between: the first needs a favourable answer
(Unresolved 1, For the owner 1), and the second is what makes the iOS
Safari `wss://` path work at all (facts, Settled). The honest cost of
click-through is in the dialog and in `docs/remote-client.md` §5: the
browser pins nothing a page can check; the URL's `key` lets a genuine page
refuse a host whose `/info` key differs, but a page served by an impostor
on the local network does not check anything, and it can relay the code to
the real host in the five-minute window. That is weaker than the native
client's pin, which §5 builds the whole pairing around. The stronger path
is to trust the certificate on the device first, from a channel other
than the one being protected.

- New `GET /api/v1/certificate`, unauthenticated, rate-limited with
  `/info`'s window, answers the DER from `identity.certificate` with
  `Content-Type: application/x-x509-ca-cert` and
  `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="switchboard-host.cer"`. It
  is public data every handshake already sends, so it adds no store and
  leaks nothing. It is inside `/api/v1/`, so the page paths stay the only
  exception to the allowlist.
- Whether iOS accepts the year-4096 `notAfter` as a trusted profile is
  Unresolved 4. This plan does not change it (follow-up 3). The page
  offers the link in its "live updates are off" state and does not depend
  on it.

### The invite URL

Decision 3. **One form, a URL.** The QR and "Copy invite" carry
`https://<address>:<port>/?code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`.
All three values are URL-safe (Crockford letters and digits, hex, a
UUID), so nothing is encoded. A new pure function
`core::remote::invite_url(identity, code, address, port) -> String`
builds it, bracketing an IPv6 address. Logic stays out of `src/ui/`.

- `PairingInvite.parse` (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:114`)
  tries a URL first and then the JSON as before. A URL gives `addresses =
  [host:port]`, `spkiSha256 = key`, `serverID = id`, `code = code`. It is
  the one entry point for every consumer the facts list: `switchboard-remote
  pair` with one argument (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:107-125`),
  `ConnectionManager.pair(invite:)`, `boot(invite:)` and the headset's
  paste field (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:849`). The
  three-argument CLI form is untouched. The JSON stays accepted, because
  `client/Fixtures/pin.json`, `pair.json` and about ten Swift tests use
  it, and an invite copied before an upgrade is still valid.

### What the page does at load

1. If `location.search` has `code`, `key`, `id`, read them into a local
   variable and call `history.replaceState(null, '', location.pathname)`
   as the first statement, before any request. The code is never stored.
2. `GET /api/v1/device`. A 200 goes straight to the sessions (the cookie
   rehydrated).
3. A 401 with a code in hand: `GET /api/v1/info`, require its `server_id`
   equal to `id` and `spki_sha256` equal to `key`, and only then
   `POST /api/v1/pair {code, spki_sha256: key, device_name, session:
   "cookie"}`. A mismatch says "this link is for a different host" and
   sends nothing. The host's own `wrong_key` check on `/pair`
   (`src/app.rs:3637`) still applies.
4. A 401 with no code: the not-paired state, with an eight-character code
   field. The page shows the short form of the key that `/info` returned,
   for the owner to compare with the dialog by eye, which is the headset's
   Bonjour path. The comparison is only as strong as that eyeball (the
   host says what it says), and the page says so in one line.

`pairing_open` in `/info` (`src/app.rs:3586`) lets the page say "pairing is
closed on the host" rather than a bare 403.

## The UI

### The page (`web/`)

No framework, no build step, no dependency. `app.js` is plain script with
no `innerHTML`: terminal text and agent replies are untrusted, so every
string goes in through `textContent`.

- **Header.** The host name (`/info.server_name`), this device's scope
  (`/device`), and a state word: "Live" when the socket is open,
  "Polling every 5 s" otherwise, with the `/api/v1/certificate` link beside
  "Polling" and one line on why.
- **List.** `GET /projects`, then `GET /projects/{id}/sessions` for each,
  with the default scope (never `scope=all`, which would add Dispatch's
  worker sessions). The page also reads `GET /waiting` and puts the waiting
  sessions in a group at the top, marked, then the projects, each with its
  waiting sessions first. A row shows name, kind, the card's word, the
  `waiting_reason` when waiting, and "quiet 4 m" from `last_activity_ms`.
- **Session.** For a Claude Code session, `GET /sessions/{id}/last-response`;
  for anything else, `GET /sessions/{id}/screen?lines=60`. On open it sends
  `watch {kind: "conversation" | "screen", id}` and refetches on the
  matching `changed`; on close, `unwatch`. A reply box appears only when
  `/device` says `control`, posts `/sessions/{id}/send {op, text}` with a
  fresh UUID for `op`, and shows `prompt_refusal` instead of the box when
  the session reports one. A `403 scope` re-reads `/device` and hides the
  box. A repeated post with the same `op` is the retry, so a dropped
  connection can resend safely (`src/app.rs:3159`).
- **Live and fallback.** The page opens `wss://<host>/api/v1/events`, waits
  for `hello`, then fetches. When the socket is not open, it polls
  `/waiting` every 5 s and refetches the list and the open session
  whenever the reply's `revision` has moved. It retries the socket every
  60 s.
- **States said plainly.** Not paired, link for a different host, identity
  changed, removed on the host, host unreachable, and pairing closed
  (above).

### The Mac's dialog (`src/ui/remote.rs`)

- The payload at line 160 becomes `invite_url(..)`. The QR, the text beside
  it and "Copy invite" (line 205) carry it.
- With `identity.listen.lan` false the QR is hidden, because the LAN
  address it names is not bound and nothing would answer (For the owner 2
  asks for exactly this). A line says "Turn on 'Allow devices on the local
  network' to pair a phone". The URL and "Copy invite" remain, with the
  loopback address, for a browser on this Mac and for the CLI.
- Under the code, one `meta_text` line: "A browser warns about this
  certificate the first time; accepting it trusts it for this address on
  that browser only. For a stronger trust, install the host's certificate
  on the device first (`/api/v1/certificate`)." Another on the radio
  choice: "A browser keeps its login in a cookie that other services on this
  IP can also receive; prefer read-only for a shared device."
- The hover text at line 113 becomes "... only paired devices get past /info,
  the certificate and the pairing page".

## The tests

Core and adapter units:

- `src/core/tests.rs`: `CertificateReissued` replaces the identity, returns
  `Effect::SaveIdentity`, leaves `devices` alone and leaves
  `identity_rotated` false; `invite_url` for IPv4, IPv6 (bracketed) and a
  port other than the default.
- `src/adapters/remote.rs`: `make_identity` records its SAN addresses and
  the DER contains each (`[0x87, 4, ..octets]`, no parser dependency is in
  the tree); `reissue_certificate` returns the same `spki_sha256`;
  `read_request` keeps `sb_session` and drops other cookies, and keeps
  `Host` and `Origin`. `src/adapters/web.rs`: every `src=`/`href=` in
  `index.html` names a served path; no inline `<script>` body, `style=`,
  `on*=` attribute, `eval(`, `innerHTML` or absolute `http(s)://` URL in
  any of the three files; the CSP string; the content types.

`tests/remote.rs` over the real listener (with an `http_full` helper beside
`http` at line 245 that returns headers, the existing one dropping them):

- The three paths answer 200 with the headers named above, `POST /` is 405,
  `/other` is the JSON 404, and 121 requests in a minute draw a 429.
- A static reply closes its connection. With three stalled strangers
  holding slots, three page fetches in a row still answer.
- Cookie pairing: `/pair` with `session: "cookie"` and a matching `Origin`
  sets a cookie with every attribute and returns no token; the cookie then
  reads `/device`, and a `GET` with no `Origin` is accepted; a `POST send`
  with no `Origin`, or an `Origin` on another port, is `403 origin`; with
  the right `Origin` it types once per `op`. A bearer plus a wrong cookie
  uses the bearer; a wrong cookie alone is 401. A pair without `session`
  is unchanged (the existing pairing tests keep passing untouched).
- The socket: an upgrade with the cookie and the right `Origin` gets
  `hello`; with no `Origin` it is 403; revoking the device closes it and
  the next `GET` is 401. This extends `subscribe_at` (line 1960) with an
  optional cookie and origin header.
- `GET /device` answers `{device_id, name, scope}` and follows
  `SetDeviceScope`; `GET /certificate` answers a DER whose SPKI hash equals
  `/info`'s with no token; after `refresh_certificate` with a different
  address, a client pinned by the old `spki_sha256` still connects and
  `devices.json` is unchanged.
- `write_fixtures` (line 1587) adds `device.json`, `pair_cookie.json` and
  `invite_url.txt`. Swift's `FixturesTests` gets a decode check only if it
  enumerates the directory (the implementer checks), and a test that
  `PairingInvite.parse` reads `invite_url.txt` and `pin.json` to the same
  fields. The Swift tests are run with `swift test` in `client/` where the
  toolchain is present, and the commit says so if it is not.

`tests/ui.rs`: the test at line 7485 now parses the copied text as a URL
(scheme `https`, `code`, `key`, `id`, and no JSON); with `lan` false there
is no QR image and the hint line is present.

Not tested by the suite, because no UI test drives a browser: the page's
JavaScript. The acceptance run below is the check, and the build order
puts the riskiest part first.

### Build order and acceptance

1. Headers channel, the 30-site conversion, `host`/`origin`/`session`,

2. SAN, `refresh_certificate`, `/certificate`, `/device`.

5. Docs: `docs/remote-client.md` §4.1 (the connection thread answers three

   (≈ line 276); `client/README.md`; `CHANGELOG.md` under `[Unreleased]`

Acceptance, as the issue words it, with the instance put in state by the
script rather than clicks (`SWITCHBOARD_SCRIPT` with `remote-listen lan
43187` and `pairing ABCD2345`, `SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` and
`SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET` pointing at short test paths): scan the QR with a
phone, accept the warning, see the sessions. Start a session waiting
(`switchboard-hook PermissionRequest` as in CLAUDE.md) and watch it move

Revoke the phone in the dialog and the page's next request says it was
removed. None of these steps needs the socket: with it blocked, the same
steps hold on polling, five seconds slower.

## For the owner, named so nothing waits on them

These are not built here (a facts line or an owner answer that would change
a spec decision is a follow-up):

1. Whether your own browsers show a proceed link for the certificate and
   whether the socket connects after it (For the owner 1). The plan works
   either way; the answer changes the dialog's wording only.
2. Which address you reach the host by (For the owner 2). The certificate
   lists the loopback names and the one outbound address. A `<name>.local`
   or a second interface is a SAN addition in `refresh_certificate`.
3. A certificate lifetime within 825 days with renewal, if iOS refuses the

4. The card's excerpt as a field on `SessionView` (needs the core to hold
   what `UiState` computes today).
5. A "forget this browser" that clears the cookie (the cookie is `HttpOnly`,
   so only the host can). Revoking from the dialog is the way until then.
6. The cookie's reach to other ports, if the owner would rather have the
   token in `sessionStorage` behind a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value. That
   trades port-blindness for script-readable storage.
7. Dispatch tickets, decisions, drafts and the longer conversation on the
   page, as the issue says.
